A year after the whole thing, Rania and Jin still worked on the same floor of the design studio in Toronto. On Friday Jin stopped by her desk with two coffees, the way he used to, and asked about her weekend.
"Went hiking with my sister," Rania said. "It was good." She didn't mention the flat she was trying to buy, or her worries about her mother's visa. Those went to Leila now, and to her sister.
They laughed about a client's font choices. It was pleasant. It was real, even. Jin had corrected what he'd said about her to the director and never repeated anything since.
But Rania had learned something about who holds what. Jin was good for coffee, for design talk, for a laugh on a slow afternoon. Not for the things that could be used.
When he left, she found she wasn't bitter. Just clear.

The staffroom at St. Anne's emptied fast after the last bell. Devika packed her marking into her bag while Wasim hovered by the kettle.
"Coffee on Saturday? Like old times?" he asked.
It had been eight months since he told the principal about her private complaint. He'd apologised, a quick "sorry if you were hurt", and then, three weeks ago, she'd heard he had passed on something about Mrs Joseph too.
Devika zipped the bag. "I don't think so, Wasim. I'm glad for the years we had. But I'm not going to keep being close."
He looked stung. "Because of one thing?"
"Because it wasn't one thing." She said it gently. She wasn't angry any more; she'd done that part in the winter.
On the way out she stopped at the library to return a book to Ms Pinto, who had become the person she called on hard days. It felt like choosing well.

qa.a: It had been eight months since he told the principal about her private complaint.

qa.a: Devika saw the pattern had repeated with Mrs Joseph, so she ended the closeness; she felt calm and gentle, no longer angry.

qa.a: Devika is honest but kind, thanks Wasim for the good years, and turns to a safer friend like Ms Pinto instead of seeking revenge.

qa.a: Wasim seems to see his betrayal as a single slip, while Devika sees a pattern; he may feel stung and not yet understand why the trust has gone.

grounding: Illustrates a woman ending a friendship without bitterness after a repeated betrayal, having learned whom she can trust with what.

Dear Omkar,

It's been four months since the promotion business, and I've been meaning to put this down properly.

I accept your apology. I believe you meant it, especially after you told Mr Sen yourself. That counted.

But I want to be honest about what our friendship looks like now. I'll still have lunch with you on Fridays. I'll still laugh at your terrible jokes. I'll help you with your presentations if you ask.

What I won't do is tell you the things I used to: what I think of the management, where I'm applying, what's happening at home. Not because I'm punishing you, but because I've learned who I can trust with what.

Maybe that will change, slowly. Maybe it won't. Either way, I'm not angry anymore. I just know my own limits better.

Warmly,
Lalremsiami

You asked if I ever made up with Uday. I'm Zeenat, and the short answer is no, and I'm at peace with that.

We'd been friends since our first job. When he told our boss about my private complaint to get ahead, I confronted him. He said sorry, but a month later I found out he'd done something similar to another colleague. That told me what I needed to know.

For a while I was bitter. I'd replay it in the shower, planning speeches.

Then one evening I just... stopped. I wrote a short message: "Thank you for the good years. I'm going to step back now. I wish you well." And I meant it.

We nod in the corridor now. That's it.

What I learned wasn't that people are bad. It's that not everyone gets the key to every room. I share different things with different people now, and that feels safer, not sadder.

qa.q: What did Zeenat write in her message to Uday?
qa.a: "Thank you for the good years. I'm going to step back now. I wish you well."

qa.q: How did Zeenat's feelings change after the betrayal?
qa.a: She was bitter for a while, replaying it and planning speeches, but later felt at peace and safer, letting him go without bitterness.

qa.q: Why was ending the friendship a sound choice here?
qa.a: Uday repeated the same behaviour with another colleague, so trust could not safely return, and Zeenat closed it with dignity.

qa.q: What might it be like for Uday to receive that message?
qa.a: He may feel ashamed or regretful, realising the friendship ended because of his pattern, not one mistake.

grounding: Zeenat describes ending a friendship with dignity after Uday repeated his betrayal, letting go without bitterness and learning who to trust with what.

I've shared a desk row with Urmila at the publishing house for two years, so I've watched the whole thing with Sneh unfold, though only from the outside.

After the fallout over the leaked manuscript, I assumed they'd never speak again. For weeks they didn't.

Then, gradually, I noticed small things. Urmila began saying good morning to Sneh again. By summer they ate lunch at the same table, though always with others around. Sneh would ask about Urmila's weekend; Urmila would answer in one line and change the subject to work.

Once I asked Urmila if they were friends again. She thought about it. "Friendly," she said. "Not friends. And that's fine."

She didn't sound bitter. She sounded like someone who had drawn a line and was comfortable standing behind it.

— Minakshi

qa.a: "Friendly. Not friends. And that's fine."

qa.a: That a cordial, careful relationship with clear limits is possible, answering personal questions briefly and keeping the connection around work, without bitterness.

qa.a: Sneh may feel a little shut out but also grateful for the civility, understanding it as a fair limit.

grounding: Minakshi, a colleague, observes Urmila rebuilding a cordial but careful relationship with Sneh after a betrayal, with clear limits and no bitterness.
